Companies that purchase Jaggaer core apps typically use ERPs and other software tools to perform their day-to-day Source to Pay activities. In some cases, users need to complete tasks that require data and services from multiple systems , and customers develop custom appl ications to accomplish this. The purpose of Jaggaer ’s ‘PaaS integration ’ is to provide a set of to ols and technique s for partners to integrate to custom applications while providing a secure, seamless and efficient experience for their users as they naviga te between Jaggaer and the custom app lications . The aim of this document is to describe Jaggaer ’s ‘PaaS integration ’ model to manage the customer specific requirements using APIs and W ebhooks provided by the JAGGAER ONE platform.

The JAGGAER ONE Platform is a centralized set of JAGGAER services that offers indu stry -standard methods to make seamless connections between JAGGAER ONE , customers, suppliers, custom applications, and cloud -based service providers.
JAGGER One Platform offers four types of integration capabilities:
• J1 Cloud Connectors
• Supplier Integrat ions
• J1 Public APIs
• J1 PaaS Connectors
In this document , we describe how to use J1 PaaS Connectors .

sections.title: 4 PaaS Integration Overview
paragraphs: J1P WS Development_Kit_PaaS Draft

PaaS is one of several products in the Jaggae r Integration Products landscape . These integration products allow customers to extend the ir Jaggaer investment , integrating Jaggaer with other applications of the customer’s IT ecosystem. Depending on the functionality required, several capabilities may be implemented in unison to deliv er a robust custom integrated application: J1 Public APIs, J1 PaaS Connectors , and J1 Identity Management. Jaggaer’s PaaS (for ‘Platform as a Service integration’ ) helps facilitate UI-level custom application integration via webhooks. PaaS is a set of webs ervice interfaces exposed to enable integration with Customer’s online application s built by JAGGAER Partners. For example, customers may have unique process compliance, user experience, or functional needs associated with their vertical industry, region, or unique organizational requirements. A Jaggaer partner would be able to leverage the PaaS integration to build a custom integration that allows a buyer to select an RFQ on a Jaggaer core app , push object data to an external web UI pa ge where the user may review it along with data from other customer applications, add details required before triggering another customer app , and then confirm the integration execution results back to t he Jaggaer core app.
4.1 PaaS Partner Responsibilities
• Jaggaer partner s will be responsible for develop ing the custom application .
• The custom application needs to be deployed and run on an external infrastructure provided by the partner or customer and hosted on the region of the customer.
• The c ustom application should manage user authorization and data segregation to ensure th at only authorized users are allowed to access or modify data when outside of the Jaggaer core app .

• Jaggaer provides a list of possible webhooks by core app . The partner will make a request to Jaggaer Global Provisioning Team (GPT) for the ones to be activated , the tenant and under what conditions , and the URL of the custom application where the user should be redirected .
4.2 J1 Public APIs and PaaS Webhooks

JAGGAER ONE platform (J1P) Public APIs enable the custome rs to integrate third -party systems with Jaggaer application s, to transfer the data from Jaggaer to the external system (customer ERPs), to transfer data from external systems to Jaggaer platform and for custom UI driven integrations developed by Jaggaer p artners. A webhook is a lightweight API that powers one -way data sharing. In conjunction with Public APIs , they enable applications to share data and functionality, and turn the web into something greater than the sum of its parts. Jaggaer is continually w orking to enhance the webhooks to manage customer specific requirements over the Webhooks integration.

4.2.1 Data export from Jaggaer to customer systems To transfer the data from Jaggaer to customer applications, Jaggaer provides three different options :

• J1P REST webservices API to allow external entities to pull data from Jaggaer either by scheduling it on customer application or invok ing the Jaggaer Public API whenever required to export the data

• Jaggaer partner middleware or EAI to pull the data from Ja ggaer using Jaggaer public API and converting the data into customer system required format before transferring it to the customer application
• Jaggaer PUSH services to push the data from Jaggaer into customer endpoint based on a configured event in Jaggaer
4.2.2 Data import from customer application to Jaggaer To transfer the data from customer application to Jaggaer, the customer application can either :
• Use J1P REST webservices API to import the data in to Jaggaer directly from a customer app
• Push the data in to partner middleware/EAI and then partner middleware/EAI convert the data into Jaggaer format and import into Jaggaer platform by using J1P REST webservices API

4.2.3 Custom UI Driven /PaaS model Integration Custom UI driven or PaaS model integr ation is used for managing the customer specific requirements. Jaggaer configurable webhooks and public APIs are used to enable flexible PaaS integration with external system s developed by Jaggaer partners.

In this section , we explain how the Jaggaer core app s and J1P collaborate to expose webhooks.
5.1 Setup

The implementation partner must identify and request activation of the webhooks required for the customer application . A list of webhooks is available in the “J1P PaaS Library and Activation Request .xls” form. It is in the same folder as thi s Development Kit you are reading. For each webhook, the implementer shall provide :
• Function requested (e.g., “RFQ”)
• Redirect URL for the custom application (e.g., “https//….)
• The Context Tag (e.g., “Status”)
• The Context Tag Value (e.g., “To be Published”)
5.2 Execution

Executi on of the Webhook -enabled integration begins in the core app and ends in the custom app. It is up to the custom app to determine what happens after the user complete s the task in the custom app and is outside the scope of this guide.

5.2.1 Core App Renders the Page and Applicable Webhook s When a user enters a core app page with Webhooks capability, the core app page interacts with the J1P Function service to determine whether any webhooks should be displayed , based on user, tenant, context, and context tags . The core app page will be rendered to the user and any applicable webhooks will be enabled.

5.2.2 User activates the Webhook The user then decides to navigate to the custom app and click s the webhook button. The core app page interacts with the J1P synchFunction service to obtain the URL of the page where the user shall be redirected and an opaque token that will be used by the custom app to authenticate itself for the next step.
5.2.3 The core app redirect s the user The Jaggaer core app takes the user to the redirection UR L. The redirection URL could look like:
https://j1p -dev -int2-reg01.de.jaggaer.com/paaspage/? a9d67305 -5e57 -4185 -8372 -292687e17a59
• https://j1p -dev -int2 -reg01.de.jaggaer.com/paaspage - this is the custo m application page that will consume the redirection
• token= a9d67305 -5e57 -4185 -8372 -292687e17a59 – this is the opaque token to be used when requesting the context (see “Custom Application retrieves the context data and proceeds with its task ”)
To achieve a secure connection communication between J1P and the external system , use HTTPS and use OAuth 2.0 for authentication .

JSON response message including created token. The following fields are defined access_token: the opaque token to be used for invoking the J1P API expires_in = the token TTL (in mseconds) refresh_expires_in = refresh_token = token_type = Bearer [segreto] = session_state = scope = Return Codes o 200 token created successfully o 400 wrong or missing data o 401 Unauthorized request (i.e. , the provided credentials are invalid)

The aim of this chapter is to describe the reference approach for implementing user authentication for PaaS Connector / Webhook -enabled applications developed by customers and partners. Jaggaer provides an authentication service implementing OpenId Connect that needs to be leveraged by external applications to authenticate users.
6.1 Reference documentation
• https://openid.net/specs/openid -connect -core -1_0.html
• https://openid.net/specs/openid -connect -session -1_0.html

6.2 OIDC Auth -Code flow Jaggaer authorization servers support OpenID connect authorization code flow ( https://openid.net/specs/openid - connect -core -1_0.html#CodeFlowAuth ). The authorization cod e flow is the most used flow, intended for traditional web apps as well as native / mobile apps. It involves an initial browser redirection to/from the OpenID Provider for user authentication and access consent, then a second back -channel request to retrie ve the (user) ID token. This flow offers optimal security, as tokens are not revealed to the browser and the client application is also authenticated. In the diagram below,
• “Client” is the PaaS custom application ; called the “Requesting Process” (RP) in the explanation below.
• “Auth Server” is the J1P Identity Manager (IDM) ; also called the “ OpenID Provider” (OP).

Step 1 – Authenticate user The RP initiates user authentication by redirecting the browser to the authorization endpoint of the OP. Example authentication redirection to the OP:

HTTP/1.1 302 Found Location : https:// auth-server/.../protocol/openid -connect/auth ? response_type=code &scope=openid &client_id=myClientId &state=af0ifjsldkj &redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fclient.example.org%2Fcb

The request parameters are encoded in the URI query: ▪ response_type – Set to code to indicate an authorization code flow. ▪ Scope – Used to specify the scope of the requested authorization in OAuth. The scope value OpenID signals a request for OpenID authentication and ID token. ▪ client_id – The client identifier of the external system at the OP. ▪ state – Opaque value set by the RP to maintain state between request and callback. ▪ redirect_uri – The RP callback URI for the authentication response.
At the OP, the user will be authenticated by checking if they have a valid session (established by a browser cookie), and in the absence of that, by prompting the user to login.
The OP will then call the client redirect_uri with an authorization code (on success) or an error code (if access was denied, or some other error occurred, such as a malformed request was detected).

The RP must validate the state parameter, and use the code to proceed to the next step —exchanging the code for the ID token.
Step 2 – Exchange code for token

The authorization code is an intermediate credential, which encodes the authorization obtained at step 1 . It is therefore opaque to the RP and only has meaning to the OP server. To retrieve the ID token , the RP must submit the code t o the OP, but this time with a direct back -channel request. This is done for two reasons:
▪ To authenticate confidential clients with the OP before revealing the tokens; ▪ To deliver the tokens straight to the RP, thus avoid ing exposing them to the browser.

The code -for-token exchange happens at the token endpoint of the OP: POST /auth/realms/ {realm -name} /protocol/openid -connect/token HTTP/1.1 Host : auth-server Content-Type : application/x -www -form -urlencoded Authorization: Basic [segreto]…nWDFmQmF0M2JW
grant_type=authorization_code &code=SplxlOBeZQQYbYS6WxSbIA &redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fclient.example.org%2Fcb
The client ID and secret are passed via the Authorization header (with basic authentication), but can also be passed as body parameters .
The token request parameters are form-encoded: ▪ grant_type – Set to authorization_code . ▪ code – The code obtained from step 1. ▪ redirect_uri – Repeats the callback URI from step 1.

Attribute Description uid This attribute exists only for supplier users . This is a Unique Identifier of the user identity inside J1. 6.3 Session Management Session management section describe a possible solution to track the session status.
• The application embeds in every page an IFrame that will track the session status.
• The IFrame URL will vary based on t he user (if supplier or buyer) and it’s dynamically generated only if the user has logged in through J1P IDM.

<iframe id="OIDC_Check_Status" src="https:// auth -server /auth/realms/{realm -name}/protocol/openid -connect/login -status - iframe.html" width="0" height="0" onload="checkSSOState();" border="0"></iframe>
• The checkSSOState function is :
• Returning the code ‘changed’ if the session is no longer active in J1P
• In case session is active , it keeps the session alive there
• If the return code of the above JS is ‘changed’ , it redirects the user to the J1App logout page
Below you can find an example of the J avaScript function checkSSOState() {

var sso_state = "" //sso_state retur ned at login time var client_id = "" //client id used for the login var iframeName= "oidcCheckIFrame" var msg = client_id + " " + sso_state; var iframe = document.getElementById('iframeName'); iframe.contentWindow.postMessage(msg, idpURL);
function handleSSOStateCheckMessage(event) {
if (event.origin !== idpURL) { return; }

if (event.data === "changed") { console.log("Redirecting to Logout Command...") window.location.href='logout page'; } else if ( event.data === "error") { console.log("Error attempting to check session") } }
